name: Olga Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Olga, thank you for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'm happy to help, as long as you don't mind the dog barking in the background.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Not at all. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit windows and doors on new-build estates, part of a three-person crew for a firm that supplies the big housebuilders. We get to site by seven, unload the frames from the van, and go house by house: fixing the frames, packing them level, sealing round them, hanging the front and back doors. On a good day we do four houses. I like it because it's tidy work, you can see it's right or wrong with a spirit level. What wears me out is the lifting, those big patio doors weigh as much as a man.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Raúl has his own plumbing business, just him and an apprentice called Ben. We have Sofía, who's fourteen, and Mateo, who's eleven. Church on Sundays, then lunch at my parents'. We've got about three months saved between us, a bit more in a good month for Raúl. I use the AI thing on my phone sometimes, to help Mateo with his maths or to check Raúl's invoices make sense before he sends them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was mostly a lot of noise from people who've never done a day's physical work. I'd say that at the school gate and after church. Not online, I don't bother with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fine by me. I'd keep using it for the little things, the homework and the invoices. My job and Raúl's would be just as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. Keep fitting windows, keep helping Raúl with his books in the evenings. Maybe we'd finally save up for the bigger van he wants, which would let him take on bathroom jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. Life's busy enough without the world turning over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about checking Raúl's invoices.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a brilliant plumber and a terrible typist. Last month he sent a customer a bill for 18 instead of 180, and the man paid it and said nothing. Now I paste them into the app and ask it to check the sums. It caught two more mistakes since. Raúl calls it his secretary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in that world that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The usual. Raúl's work is up and down, and the housing market makes my work up and down too. If people stop building, we both feel it at once. That's the worry, not computers.

S0.say: It was mostly noise from people who've never done a day's physical work. I'd say that at the school gate and after church, but not online.
S0.think: It's fine by me, because I'd keep using it for homework and invoices. My job and Raúl's would carry on just as they are.
S0.do: Carries on fitting windows and doors and doing her husband's books in the evenings. Saves toward the bigger van he needs to take on bathroom jobs.
S0.quote: He's a brilliant plumber and a terrible typist.
S0.fieldNote: Olga's household runs on her steady wage plus her husband's small business. She uses AI for small practical jobs and sees no threat in a plateau. Her worry is that housing slowdowns hit both of them at once. Family and church anchor her week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every generation has had to adjust, and we'll manage like they did. The government should get out of the way and let firms train people properly, with apprenticeships, not schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the windows will come pre-fitted in factory walls more and more. That's already happening on some sites. A three-person crew could become a one-person crew with a machine. I'm not the fastest on our crew, so I know who'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the firm does, and once one of the other crews tries a new lifting machine or fixing robot, I'd ask to train on it. I'd start doing more of Raúl's quoting with AI, so if his business grew I could step into it. And we'd save a bit more each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the back of my head when I'm driving home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not the fastest. Who is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kerry, our lead fitter. She can do a front door in twenty minutes. Then there's Darius, who's young and strong. I'm the careful one. That used to be worth something, but a machine is careful too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you and Raúl talked about you joining his business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've joked about it. He says he'd have to pay me, which he can't afford. But if his business grew, maybe. I'd do the office side and help on the bigger jobs. I'd want it to be a real decision, not something we fall into.

S1.say: Every generation has had to adjust and we'll manage like they did. The government should get out of the way and let firms train people with proper apprenticeships, not schemes.
S1.think: I think windows will come pre-fitted in factory-made walls more and more, so a three-person crew could become one person with a machine. I'm not the fastest on our crew, so I know who'd go.
S1.do: Asks to train on new lifting or fixing machines once another crew has tried them. Takes on more of her husband's quoting using AI so she could step into his business, and saves a little more each month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with it at the back of her mind on the drive home.
S1.quote: I'm the careful one. That used to be worth something, but a machine is careful too.
S1.fieldNote: Olga sees her husband's business as a possible lifeboat, which is unusual among workers here. She is candid about being the slowest on her crew. Her traditional outlook shows in wanting apprenticeships over government schemes. She will adopt new machines once others prove them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big companies rushed this out to make money without thinking about families. I'd say it after church and at the school gate. And I'd say we need to look after each other, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. Two years, and robots can fit windows and fix pipes too. That's my job and Raúl's business both gone, and the business was supposed to be our safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, we'd stop all the extras: the summer trip to my sister's, Sofía's guitar lessons, eating out. We'd hold off on the van completely. I'd go into Raúl's business full time and push him to take every job he can while there's still work, saving everything we can. And we'd lean on family and the church, my parents have offered before, and I'd swallow my pride and say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That kind of fear where you keep checking the bank app at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to Ben, the apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what breaks my heart. Ben is nineteen, he's just learning, he's a good lad. Raúl would want to keep him, but you can't pay someone with no work. Raúl would take it harder than losing his own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government support if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there was nothing else, yes, for the children. I'd rather it was a loan or something I could pay back. I don't like the idea of just being given money. But I'm not going to let Mateo go hungry over pride.

S2.say: The big companies rushed this out to make money without thinking about families. We need to look after each other, because nobody else will.
S2.think: I'd be frightened, because robots could fit windows and fix pipes within two years. My job and Raúl's business would both go, and the business was supposed to be our safety net.
S2.do: Cuts extras straight away, including a summer trip, her daughter's guitar lessons and eating out, and drops plans for the van. Joins her husband's business full time to take every job while it lasts, saves everything she can, and accepts help from her parents and church.
S2.feel: Alarmed, checking the bank app at night.
S2.quote: That's my job and Raúl's business both gone, and the business was supposed to be our safety net.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture removes Olga's lifeboat as well as her job, which is what alarms her. She blames large companies for rushing, not government. She'd accept help from family and church first, and government support only for her children's sake, ideally as a loan. Her concern for the apprentice was tender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this right if people take responsibility. Families, businesses, churches, all of us. Not wait for someone in the capital to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives Raúl's business a few good years, maybe. People will still need a plumber they trust until the robots are cheap. And I'd have time to learn the office side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an evening bookkeeping course at the college, maybe 300 for the year, so I could run Raúl's paperwork properly. I'd keep fitting windows for another two or three years while we save, then move into the business. I'd use the AI more for quotes and ordering, so we can do more jobs with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. There's a plan, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait two or three years before moving into the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my wage is the steady one. Raúl's money goes up and down. If I jump too early and the business has a bad winter, we're in trouble. I want to see it grow first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sofía about her future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's fourteen, she'd be nineteen when it lands. I'd say stay close to family, learn something useful, and don't take on huge debts for a degree that might not mean anything by then. I'm not sure that's right, but it's what I'd say.

S3.say: There's time to do this right if people take responsibility: families, businesses, churches, all of us. We shouldn't wait for someone in the capital to fix it.
S3.think: Five years gives Raúl's business a few good years, since people will still want a plumber they trust until robots are cheap. I'd have time to learn the office side properly.
S3.do: Takes an evening bookkeeping course at the college for about 300 a year and keeps fitting windows for two or three years while the family saves. Then moves into her husband's business, using AI for quotes and ordering so they can do more with fewer people.
S3.feel: Anxious but not frozen, steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: My wage is the steady one. Raúl's money goes up and down.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Olga builds a careful plan around the family business, keeping her steady wage until the business proves itself. She stresses responsibility from families and communities rather than the state. Her advice to her daughter about debt reflects her caution. She admits she isn't sure it's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for families and businesses to prepare. The government should back apprenticeships and small firms, and otherwise leave people to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'd be 53, my back would be glad to stop lifting patio doors. If Raúl's business is doing well, I could move into it fully. The children would be through school. I think we'd be okay, as long as people still want a person under their sink for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting for a few more years, do the bookkeeping course, and build up Raúl's business with him. I'd learn the AI tools properly for the office side. And I'd help Sofía and Mateo pick something practical, maybe a trade that works alongside the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. Ten years feels like a proper chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said as long as people want a person under their sink. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. I'd be 53 or so, and we'd have savings and a paid-down house, God willing. We'd manage the way families always have, by sticking together. I can't plan past that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He loves fixing things, takes his bike apart every weekend. I'd tell him to do an apprenticeship and learn the machines too. And to keep going to church, because whatever happens, he'll need people around him.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time for families and businesses to prepare. The government should back apprenticeships and small firms and otherwise leave people to get on with it.
S4.think: At 53 my back would be glad to stop lifting patio doors, and I could move into Raúl's business fully. We'd be okay as long as people still want a person under their sink for a while.
S4.do: Keeps fitting windows for a few more years, takes the bookkeeping course and builds up her husband's business with him. Learns AI tools properly for the office side and guides her children toward practical trades that work alongside machines.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, feeling ten years is a proper chance.
S4.quote: I think we'd be okay, as long as people still want a person under their sink for a while.
S4.fieldNote: A decade lets Olga plan a gradual move into the family business while her children finish school. She stays uneasy because she can't see past the point where people stop wanting human tradespeople. Faith and family are her backstop. Her advice to her son combines an apprenticeship with learning the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the business we were counting on would go down with my job. What would help is support for small family firms, like cheaper loans or tax breaks, so they can adapt instead of going under, and apprenticeships for the young ones like Ben.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith. People keep asking about money, but when things go wrong, it's the church and the family that hold you up. Somebody should ask what happens to those if everybody's out of work at once.

headlineQuote: Last month he sent a customer a bill for 18 instead of 180, and the man paid it and said nothing.
portrait: Olga is a 43-year-old window and door fitter on new-build estates, married to a self-employed plumber, with two children and about three months of savings. She uses AI now and then for homework and checking her husband's invoices. She sees his business as the family's safety net and plans to move into it as change comes. The fast AGI picture alarms her because both her job and that safety net would go at once. With more time she builds a careful plan around bookkeeping and the family firm, leaning on family, faith and self-reliance.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her husband's business, the family's safety net, would fail along with her job.
whatWouldHelp: Support for small family firms, such as cheaper loans or tax breaks, so they can adapt, and apprenticeships for young workers.
